newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S KWV SAYS COURT DELAY COULD COST DEARLY.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S KWV SAYS COURT DELAY COULD COST DEARLY.

text.p: South Africa's KWV wine and spirits co-operative said on Wednesday that it could lose juicy foreign contracts because of attempts by Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom to block its conversion to a public company.
Lawyers for KWV told the Cape Town Supreme Court, which is hearing the co-operative's application to convert to a company, that KWV had "vigorous" international expansion plans.
"Business is not static, and that's the urgency," KWV lawyer Philip Ginsberg said.
"If this case is delayed, KWV will miss very fruitful business opportunities abroad, which could earn the country sorely needed foreign exchange," the lawyer said.

KWV, which as a co-operative is the statutory regulator of the wine and spirits industry in South Africa, is active in about 50 foreign countries. It had intended to complete its transformation into a company by the end of this month.
Hanekom is seeking permission from the court to intervene in the planned KWV restructuring, saying among other things that some of the co-operative's assets could be state property.
Hanekom's legal advisor Steven Goldblatt estimated these assets at around four billion rand, saying they included the world's biggest stocks of 15-year-old brandy.

Other lawyers for Hanekom said the assets included secret information on South African vine plantings like what cultivars were planted in what quantities and the historic production figures for many wine estates.

KWV, which had obtained this information in its role as regulator of the industry, would use it for commercial gain as a public company in what would amount to unfair competition with other players in the market, the lawyers told the court.
Ginsberg said the assets obtained by KWV to carry out its regulatory duties were "insignificant" and said the co-operative had no intention of competing in the local market.

He rejected submissions by lawyers for Hanekom that KWV's change of identity would leave the South African wine and spirits industry in a legal vacuum with no regulatory body, calling them "startling and absurd".

Ginsberg said that under the terms of the planned conversion, KWV would pay back to its members all its paid-up share capital. It would then take the money back in exchange for shares in the new company.
"KWV is giving with its left hand and taking back with its right hand. So the hysteria surrounding this scheme and the alleged enrichment of wine farmers is fallacious," Ginsberg said.
The hearing was adjourned to Thursday.
